item.title: Slides: the previous window as a prior
item.description: These slides are the illustrated companion to
item.content:encoded:
These slides are the illustrated companion to the write-up. The registered rule's output is not shown, at this size, with no harm. Beside the rule, carrying the previous window's state as a prior gives a small average shift: about 10% in geometric mean and 3% in the median window. Spec: specs/028-carry-prior/.

What was built​

  • src/tma2/long/carried.py: the carried prior.
    • The fit and evidence carry it as a Gaussian term. With no prior they equal the originals, which a unit test checks.
    • The hand-over excludes the next window's bearings.
    • It also holds the widening and the χ²(4) guard.
  • src/tma2/long/carry2.py: ctl-prior beside ctl and ctl-carry in one job. A test checks that ctl and ctl-carry equal spec 026's.
  • src/tma2/long/study27.py: the scorer. CLI: tma2-long carry2, study27 and jointpair.
  • CI: long.yml now ignores pushes to main and pushes its results to an orphan branch.
  • Records:
    • tuning experiments/20261118-cp-tuning/;
    • decision 20261119-cp-decision/;
    • validation 20261119-cp-val/;
    • test 20261119-cp/, with review.md, supplement.json and ties.json.

What was not achieved​

  • The owner's case: a window without useful ownship geometry does not occur in this simulator.
  • Gain on the registered split: not shown.
  • Whether the prior narrows the set of histories: not tested.
  • The hand-over defect: the refit's start is recorded, not repaired.

What comes next (the owner's choice)​

  • Recommended: adopt ctl-prior with its guard for tended contacts up to 12 hours, then close the track.
  • Alternatives:
    • an ownship that holds course for one to two hours, which answers the owner's question directly;
    • a registered joint solve over consecutive windows.

Figures: scripts/research/cp_charts.py, with a sidecar beside each SVG.

item.title: Long engagements: the previous window as a prior
item.description: Spec 026 found that handing the previous 2-hour window's track to the next window as a starting
item.content:encoded:
Spec 026 found that handing the previous 2-hour window's track to the next window as a starting guess changed nothing in accuracy. The owner expected more: "knowledge of the previous track can usefully constrain the range of permutations for this leg".

This study tests that expectation as a prior. The previous window hands on its estimate of the target's position, course and speed at the next window's first row, with its uncertainty. That estimate enters the next window's fit and the evidence that ranks manoeuvre histories.

The registered rule's output is not shown, at this size, with no harm anywhere. Beside the rule, the prior gives a small average shift: about 10% in geometric mean and 3% in the median window. Spec: specs/028-carry-prior/. Record: experiments/20261119-cp/.

What was registered​

Design (decision record experiments/20261119-cp-decision/, before seeds 355 and 356 existed):

  • Systems: ctl, ctl-carry (spec 026's carried start) and ctl-prior are solved on every window of a chain, in one job per contact.
  • The hand-over:
    • The carried estimate uses no bearing the next window also uses.
    • Its Laplace covariance is scaled by 4 and widened for manoeuvres the earlier bearings could not yet show.
    • A χ²(4) guard drops the prior where the window's own bearings reject it.

The rule: ctl ÷ ctl-prior per window, with the engagement bootstrap and each chain's first window excluded.

  • Gain: the lower limit is above 1 on windows of weak geometry: the untended contact, a window near a contact gap, or one with at most one ownship turn.
  • Harm: an upper limit is below 1 on any split, in range, course or speed.

What happened​

Test (seed 356, 60 realistic engagements of 6 and 12 hours, both contacts, scored once):

splitctl ÷ ctl-prior, range
weak geometry (registered)1.105 [0.963, 1.273]
other windows of the tended contact1.14 [1.035, 1.27]
tended contact1.11 [1.006, 1.22]
untended contact1.16 [0.988, 1.37]

The panel's sensitivities do not change the outcome:

  • clustered by engagement, the weak split is 1.105 [0.951, 1.279];
  • without the 13 windows where nothing was handed on, it is 1.112 [0.964, 1.297].

Soundness:

  • 720 of 720 windows ran.
  • On the tended contact, the carried 95% region covered the truth 95.3% of the time.

What the panel narrowed​

The panel was three reviewers, each approve with findings (experiments/20261119-cp/review.md).

  • The owner's case was not sampled. The ownship turns every 20–40 minutes, so a window with no useful ownship manoeuvre never occurs in this simulator. The weak split is in effect the untended contact plus windows near gaps. On the gap windows of the tended contact the ratio is 0.98 [0.79, 1.25].
  • What the prior does, beside the rule:
    • About 1.1 in geometric mean on the tended contact's ordinary windows, in range and course, on validation and test.
    • The median window is 1.03 and 44% of windows are worse. That is an average shift with many losses.
    • It is not concentrated where the declared manoeuvre count changed. Whether the same history was kept was not tested.
    • So "narrows the permutations" is not shown, either way.
  • The prior against the carried start alone: ctl-carry ÷ ctl-prior is 1.14 to 1.22 on every split. On this seed ctl-carry itself was level with ctl (0.95).
  • The guard did what it was for. It fell back on 8 of 443 windows. There, the unguarded answer was 1.85 times ctl's error.
  • Forecasts: two of five were wrong, the other split's sign and the coverage level. Twelve tuning engagements had no forecast value.
  • Registration:
    • The registered settings were extrapolated from a grid, not run as a chain on tuning.
    • The coverage check covered only the tended contact, while the decided split is mostly the untended one (coverage 0.76 on validation).
  • A recorded defect: the hand-over's refit starts from the full window's fit. On flat valleys it can keep information from the overlap, counting those bearings twice. At this study's scale coverage did not show it.

What it costs​

The prior's searches add about 24% to the run's search time. The fit told the true manoeuvre history is still 0.72 to 0.86 times ctl-prior's error. On 12 tuning pairs, spec 025's joint solve over two windows was 1.7 times better, at three times the time.

Next (the owner's choice)​

  • Recommended default: adopt ctl-prior, with its guard, as the standing chained system for tended contacts up to 12 hours, scoped as "a small refinement, no harm shown". Then close the long-engagement track as a simulation study.
  • The test that answers the owner's question: a simulator option where the ownship holds course for one to two hours, with ctl-prior scored there. It is cheap.
  • The larger lead: a registered joint solve over consecutive windows. It is 1.7 times better on 12 pairs, at three times the cost.

Slides: the slides post.

item.description: The illustrated companion to the spec 027 write-up: the
item.content:encoded:
The illustrated companion to the spec 027 write-up: the registered comparison, how often the carry changes anything, and where.

What the figures show​

  • Verdict: carry ÷ joint and alone ÷ carry in range on every split, periods after an engagement's first, with 95% engagement intervals.
  • Ties: the share of later periods where the carry is within 1% of ctl alone, better or worse.
  • Kinds: alone ÷ carry for periods with and without an ownship turn of their own.

Reproducing the figures​

uv run python scripts/research/tl9_charts.py --record experiments/20261119-tl9 --out-dir site/static/img/2026-11-19-carry-across-gaps-slides

The script reads only the committed record (results branch results/timelate-tl-m-test-44440932257, seed 361); each figure's .json sidecar names the inputs' digests and the commit.

item.title: Carrying state across gaps: a carried start does not substitute for joining
item.description: Spec 025 showed that one solve over several periods of a target beats solving each period
item.content:encoded:
Spec 025 showed that one solve over several periods of a target beats solving each period alone. The cheaper habit is to solve period by period and hand each answer on to the next. This registered study measured that habit against the joint solve. By the rule registered beforehand, joining is better on Annex B targets, and the carry shows no effect over solving alone there. The review panel approved and narrowed the result. What was tested is a carried start, not carried information, so the study says nothing yet about carrying a prior. Nothing was trained. The illustrated companion is the slides post.

What was built​

The carry solves each period in order, on that period's own bearings. In the standing control ctl, the search starts from two places: C″'s answer and a start from nothing. The carry replaces the start from nothing with the previous period's declared state at its last row, run forward at constant velocity through the gap. Everything else is ctl, as spec 024 designed its carry for overlapping windows. With no carried state the code reproduces ctl exactly, and every run checks this on each engagement's first period. Spec 024's own carry was not run: it carries over rows that windows share, and across a gap there are none.

How it was decided​

All comparisons are over periods after an engagement's first, on spec 025's rows. Each is a per-period ratio of period median range error, with a 95% interval from resampling engagements.

  • Carry ÷ joint: "joining better" if the interval is wholly above 1, "carry better" if wholly below.
  • Alone ÷ carry: "carrying helps" if the interval is wholly above 1; "carrying harms" if the interval is wholly below 1 in range, course or speed.

Annex B decides.

  • Seeds: tuning on spent seed 353, validation 360 (soundness passed), test 361, scored once.

The result​

splitcarry ÷ jointalone ÷ carry
Annex B (decides)2.33 [1.66, 3.43]: joining better1.07 [0.88, 1.34]: not shown
busier targets1.351 [0.993, 1.820]: not separated1.29 [1.09, 1.54]: helps
2% wild bearings3.57 [2.21, 5.68]: joining better1.10: not shown
held course10.5 [5.5, 19.8]: joining better1.27: not shown

No harm on any split in any quantity. The joint solve stays the standing system for several periods of one target, within spec 025's conditions.

What it means, as the panel narrowed it​

  • Joining had to win. Nothing from the earlier period enters the period's likelihood or prior; only where the search starts changes. Even the per-period fit told the true manoeuvre history is 8.4 times worse than joining on these rows (Annex B). So the study shows where the information is. It does not show what carrying, done properly, is worth.
  • The carry rarely changes the answer. About half of later periods end exactly where ctl alone does. On busier targets the carry helps in about a quarter of periods, about twice as good there, almost all where the period has no ownship turn of its own (1.72). That is a different minimum of a poorly determined fit, not an answer the bearings endorse.
  • No harm shown, which is not the same as no cost. Annex B periods with their own turn read 0.91 [0.78, 1.02]. A wrong carried state replaces the start from nothing, which is the carry's only way to do harm.
  • Busier targets. The range interval misses "joining better" by 0.007; joining is better in course and speed. For a busier period that stands alone, neither joining (spec 025: 1.06) nor carrying is shown to help.
  • No recommendation. The first record recommended the carry where a joint solve is unavailable. The rule recommends it only if it helps on Annex B, which it does not, so the recommendation is withdrawn.
  • What "not shown" excludes. On Annex B the interval rules out harm worse than about 12% and gains above about a third, and nothing smaller.

Forecasts​

Right:

  • joining better on Annex B (about 2.2; 2.33);
  • carrying not shown on Annex B;
  • carrying helping a little on busier targets (1.29, larger than forecast).

Wrong:

  • joining better on busier targets (not separated, by a hair);
  • held course about 4 (it was 10.5);
  • a harm in held-course speed (none).

What was not done​

  • A carried prior.
  • A test of the carry chain in the unit tests.
  • IMM and EKF tracks.

What next (the owner's choice)​

The panel's order:

  1. A carried prior. The previous period's state and covariance, widened through the gap by Annex B's manoeuvre rates, used as a prior in the period's evidence. Scored on spent seeds first, this decides whether joining is needed at all.
  2. A consistency flag. A per-period flag for a failed join, and markers on inferred gap manoeuvres.
  3. An uncertainty. A stated uncertainty for the joined track.
  4. Longer gaps. Gaps longer than 30 minutes.

Records: decision experiments/20261118-tl9-decision/, tuning 20261118-tl9-tuning/, validation 20261118-tl9-val/, test 20261119-tl9/ with the panel's review.md. Spec specs/027-carry-across-gaps/.

item.title: Kickoff: carrying the previous window as a prior
item.description: Spec 026's ctl-carry gave each 2-hour window the previous window's track as a starting guess.
item.content:encoded:
Spec 026's ctl-carry gave each 2-hour window the previous window's track as a starting guess. It found the same answers faster but no better ones, because nothing in the fit itself changed. The owner expected knowledge of the previous track to narrow the hypotheses for the next window. This study tests that expectation directly. The previous window's estimate and its uncertainty enter the next window's fit, and the evidence that ranks manoeuvre histories, as a prior. Spec: specs/028-carry-prior/.

Where we are​

  • Spec 026's registered study found carrying a starting guess level with solving each window cold. The ratio was 1.021 [0.950, 1.100] without the first windows, which are equal by construction. The search was 31% cheaper. A gain of up to about 10% was not excluded.
  • The standing time-late system is ctl. It scores 1.5–2.2% median range error on a tended contact and 1.3–1.5 times worse on an untended one.
  • Spec 025 showed what a real constraint across time can win. Solving periods jointly gained about 3× on Annex B targets, mostly where a period had no ownship turn of its own.

Where this task moves to​

  • SRD §1. A registered study, not a gate. Nothing is trained and nothing runs on GPU.
  • Rule: gain if the geometric mean of ctl ÷ ctl-prior per window has its lower limit above 1 on the weak-geometry split. Weak geometry means the untended contact, a window after a contact gap, or a window with at most one ownship turn. Harm if any split's upper limit is below 1, in range, course or speed. Each chain's first window is excluded.
  • Safeguards:
    • the carried estimate uses no bearing the next window also uses;
    • its uncertainty is widened for manoeuvres it cannot yet see;
    • a chi-square guard drops the prior where the window's bearings reject it.
  • Plan:
    1. build ctl-prior beside ctl and ctl-carry, solved in the same job;
    2. tune the widening and the guard's level on seed 354, and check the weak-geometry split has at least 100 windows;
    3. write the decision record and its forecasts;
    4. validate on seed 355, including a coverage check of the carried prior;
    5. score the test on seed 356 (30 + 30 engagements of 6 and 12 hours) once;
    6. run the agent review panel, then publish the write-up.
  • Risks:
    • Laplace covariances have been overconfident before. An overconfident prior pulls each window towards the last window's mistakes.
    • A Gaussian prior on one state cannot hand on a second-best manoeuvre history.
    • A gain confined to the untended contact would describe this simulator.
  • Stop: the study stops before the test if the carried prior's coverage falls outside its declared band, or if spec 026's soundness checks fail on validation.

How progress will be shown​

  • ctl ÷ ctl-prior per window, by split and contact, with the registered interval against 1.
  • The prior's own effect, ctl-carry ÷ ctl-prior, window by window along a chain.
  • The carried prior's 95% coverage and the guard's fall-back rate.
  • A track plot of one weak-geometry chain: truth, ctl, ctl-prior.
  • All from the test record on seed 356, with tuning seed 354 for the design figures.

item.title: Slides: long engagements, the registered study
item.description: These slides are the illustrated companion to
item.content:encoded:
These slides are the illustrated companion to the registered study's write-up. Each rule gave its registered output:

  • E1, carrying state: non-inferior by 0.008;
  • E2, the untended contact: about 1.5 times worse where it is held;
  • E3, IMM drift: not shown.

The panel narrowed all three. Spec: specs/026-long-study/.

What was built​

  • The estimands (src/tma2/long/study.py): E1 to E3, the soundness checks and a bootstrap over engagements. They were registered in experiments/20261118-ls-decision/ with the run files and code bound by digest.
  • An IMM runner over whole engagements (long/realtime.py imm_states), with the CLI parts tma2-long imm and tma2-long study.
  • The study configs configs/long/study-{tuning,val,test}.json (seeds 349, 350, 351).
  • The records: tuning, validation and test (experiments/20261118-ls*), the panel's review.md and supplement.json (scripts/research/long_study_supplement.py).

What was not achieved​

  • No accuracy gain from carrying state was shown.
  • E2 and E3 describe this simulator, whose realism is set by hand.
  • Mis-association is not exercised.

What comes next (the owner's choice)​

Recommended: stop the long-engagement track here as a simulation study, and keep ctl-carry as an optional cost measure for tended contacts up to 12 hours. Reopen it only with measured realism, an ownship steered by its own track, or association.

Figures: scripts/research/long_study_charts.py, with a sidecar beside each SVG.

item.title: Long engagements: the registered study
item.description: A registered study on fresh seeds: 60 realistic engagements of 6 and 12 hours, scored once.
item.content:encoded:
A registered study on fresh seeds: 60 realistic engagements of 6 and 12 hours, scored once. Each rule returned what it was registered to return:

  • carrying state between time-late windows is non-inferior, by 0.008;
  • the contact the ownship does not tend is about 1.5 times worse where it is held;
  • the IMM's drift is not shown.

The review panel narrowed all three. The long-engagement track is recommended to stop here as a simulation study. Spec: specs/026-long-study/; record: experiments/20261118-ls/.

What was registered​

Before seeds 350 and 351 existed, the decision record (experiments/20261118-ls-decision/) bound the estimands, the run files and the code by digest.

  • E1: on the tended contact, the per-window ratio of ctl's median range error to ctl-carry's. Carry is non-inferior if the geometric mean's 95% interval has a lower limit of at least 0.95.
  • E2: on the untended contact against the tended one, in range bands. A magnitude.
  • E3: the IMM's median error in hours 6–12 against hours 0–6. Drift is shown if the interval lies above 1.
  • Soundness, on validation (seed 350): windows ran; ctl is sane against the true-history fit; bearings are held a realistic share of the time. It passed.

What the test returned (seed 351)​

estimate95% intervalrule's output
E11.017[0.958, 1.082]non-inferior
E21.47[1.12, 2.05]a magnitude
E31.06[0.82, 1.31]not shown

Soundness passed again: 360 of 360 windows ran; ctl ÷ the reference was 1.36; bearings were held 0.85 of the time.

What it may be taken to mean (panel, round 1)​

E1: the rule's yes rests on level windows.

  • 60 of the 359 windows are each chain's first, where ctl-carry is ctl, and 113 more come out identical.
  • Without the first windows the estimate is 1.021 [0.9502, 1.100], 0.0002 above the line.
  • Where the two systems differ, it is 1.034 [0.923, 1.168]: not shown to be within 5%.
  • At 12 hours alone it is 1.005 [0.923, 1.096]. On the untended contact it is 0.942 [0.880, 1.007], twice worse in 16 windows and twice better in 7.
  • Carrying is therefore adopted only as a cost measure, and only for the tended contact on 6–12 hour engagements. It saves 31% of the search where it runs, about 7% of all CPU. It is not recommended for an untended contact.

E2: a description of this simulator, not "the cost of an untended contact".

  • The second target has no range keeping. It is scored only where it is detected, which is 61% of its rows.
  • Within a band it sits farther out than the tended one. In 2-km sub-bands the ratio is 1.34 [1.01, 1.87].
  • Bearing rate and ownship manoeuvres are not matched. Mis-association is not exercised: 314 swapped bearings in about 389,000.
  • The forecast of 1.2–1.4 assumed range banding would remove most of the geometry. It did not.

E3: says nothing about failures.

  • The share of rows the IMM answers falls from 0.91 to 0.74–0.79.
  • With unanswered rows counted as failures, the ratio is 1.26 [0.88, 1.80]. The interval does not exclude a 30% rise.
  • What is shown is fewer answers later on, not a stable error.

Known limits​

  • The realism parameters (gaps, detection, the steering error) are spec 024's choices, not measured. The ownship steers on a fresh noisy draw of the truth, not on any estimator's track.
  • The shards ran on seven CPU families. E2 compares two jobs.
  • The panel's minor findings, all in review.md:
    • S1 counted one window that gave no answer;
    • the weighting is by window;
    • provenance details.

What comes next (the owner's choice)​

Recommended: stop the long-engagement track here as a simulation study, with ctl-carry recorded as an optional cost measure for tended contacts up to 12 hours. More registered studies on hand-set realism would measure the parameters, not the systems.

Reopen the track only with one of three things:

  • measured gap, detection and association statistics;
  • an ownship steered by the estimator's own track;
  • a tracker that handles association.

The slides: long engagements: the registered study, slides.

item.title: Kickoff: long engagements, a registered study
item.description: The owner chose note 13's registered study. On fresh seeds, with the questions fixed before
item.content:encoded:
The owner chose note 13's registered study. On fresh seeds, with the questions fixed before any result, it asks three things:

  • is carrying state between time-late windows no worse than solving each window cold;
  • how much worse the standing control does on a contact the ownship does not tend;
  • whether the IMM drifts over twelve hours.

Spec: specs/026-long-study/.

Where we are​

Spec 024 built the three recommendations of note 12 on four engagements:

  • carrying state was level in accuracy and cheaper in search;
  • the incremental C was not adopted;
  • an untended contact was three to five times worse where it could be solved at all.

All of these are anecdotes from one engagement per length.

Where this task moves to​

  • E1: ctl-carry is non-inferior to ctl if the lower limit of the geometric mean of per-window ratios is at least 0.95. Read on the tended contact.
  • E2: the cost of an untended contact, banded by range. A magnitude, with no rule.
  • E3: the IMM's drift over 12 hours. Shown if the interval lies above 1.
  • Plan:
    1. a tuning run on seed 349, giving forecasts;
    2. the decision record, binding the plan and code by digest before seeds 350 and 351 exist;
    3. validation on seed 350, with soundness checks;
    4. the test on seed 351 (30 + 30 realistic engagements of 6 and 12 hours), scored once;
    5. the agent review panel, then the write-up.
  • Risks: E1 may be inconclusive at this size. E2 confounds geometry with tending, by design. E3 reads one IMM tuning.

How progress will be shown​

The slides post will carry:

  • E1's per-window ratios against the 0.95 line;
  • E2's ratio by range band;
  • E3's error and share answered by 2-hour bin, with the intervals.

item.title: Slides: long engagements, carrying state, an incremental C, realism
item.description: Note 12's three recommendations, built and measured on the same four engagements. Carrying state
item.content:encoded:
Note 12's three recommendations, built and measured on the same four engagements. Carrying state between time-late windows makes the search cheaper but not more accurate. The incremental C is 1.7 times cheaper but loses accuracy, so it is not adopted. With realism, the contact the ownship tends keeps its accuracy, and a contact it does not tend drifts away and is three to five times worse where it can be solved at all. An investigation, not a gate. Spec: specs/024-long-carry-incremental-realism/.

What was built​

  • ctl-carry (src/tma2/long/carry.py): the standing control with its start from nothing replaced by the previous window's declared track and manoeuvres. It is solved beside ctl on every window, and that ctl equals spec 023's runner within 1 mm.
  • An incremental C (src/tma2/long/incremental.py): one confirmation per 2-hour block of estimates, cropped to each estimate's window. With blocks of one it equals the per-window run.
  • Realism (configs/long/realistic.json): the ownship steers on what it measures; contact gaps; detection fading with range; a second contact with mis-association where the two cross. It is drawn from its own random stream, so contact 1 is spec 023's target.
  • A set selector on the long-engagement sections of the viewer and the time-late page, research note 13, and the record experiments/20261117-long2/.

What was found​

  • Carry: the median ratio of ctl to ctl-carry per window is 1.00 in every set. Wins and losses are mixed: 15 to 20 on spec 023's engagements, 22 to 11 on realistic contact 1. The start from the carry costs about 55% of the search it replaces.
  • Incremental C: E and C″ cost 32–42 s an estimate against 53–73 s per window. Median range error is worse at 24 and 48 hours (E 29.8% and 35.6% against 14.3% and 20.9%).
    • The first estimate of each block matches the per-window run.
    • The later ones are 2 to 4 times worse.
    • The cause lies in the longer history before the crop and is not established.
  • Realism:
    • Contact 1 is held 67–85% of the time, and ctl stays at 1.5–2.2% (spec 023's: 1.6–2.1%).
    • Contact 2 drifts to a median 27–147 km and is held 10–22% of the time beyond 6 hours. On the windows with at least five minutes of its bearings, ctl is at 6–8%, and the true-history fit is at 2–4.5%.

What was not achieved​

  • No accuracy gain from carrying state, and the incremental C is not usable as built.
  • Mis-association is barely exercised (0–8 swapped bearings an engagement).
  • One engagement per length: these are anecdotes, not rates.

What comes next (the owner's choice)​

Recommended: a registered study on 6- and 12-hour realistic engagements (seeds 349 to 351, about 160 CPU-hours). It would test carry non-inferiority, the cost of an untended contact and the IMM's drift. Or measure shorter incremental blocks on tuning data first, or stop the long-engagement track here.

Figures: scripts/research/long2_charts.py, with a sidecar beside each SVG.

item.title: Kickoff: carrying state across gaps, against joining through them
item.description: Spec 025 showed that one solve over several periods of a target beats solving each alone. The
item.content:encoded:
Spec 025 showed that one solve over several periods of a target beats solving each alone. The cheaper thing an analyst would do instead is to solve period by period and hand each answer on to the next. This task measures that carry against the joint solve, as a registered study on fresh seeds (owner, option B). Nothing is trained.

Where we are​

  • Spec 025: the joint solve gains on every split (Annex B 3.10 [2.22, 4.58]), mostly by making periods without their own ownship turn answerable; its panel asked first for a comparison with carrying state.
  • Spec 024 (another session) built ctl-carry for overlapping windows; across a gap it has nothing to carry, so it is not this comparison.

Where this task moves to​

  • Spec specs/027-carry-across-gaps/. Carry: each later period starts its search from the previous period's declared state, run forward at constant velocity through the gap.
  • Registered: carry ÷ joint (is joining better?) and alone ÷ carry (does carrying help?), per split, with engagement intervals.
  • Plan: build the carry and test that without a carried start it equals ctl; tune on spent seed 353; decision record; validation seed 360; test seed 361; panel; write-up.
  • Risk: a manoeuvre in the gap makes the carried state wrong, and a carry can only start a fit that uses the period's own bearings, so a period without its own turn may stay unanswerable.

How progress will be shown​

  • Charts of carry ÷ joint and alone ÷ carry by split, by kind of period and on rows a period determines alone; one engagement's tracks with all three systems.

item.title: Slides: time-late over several periods of one target, joined through the gaps
item.description: The illustrated companion to the spec 025 write-up: one
item.content:encoded:
The illustrated companion to the spec 025 write-up: one engagement as tracks, the registered verdict, where the gain comes from, manoeuvres in the gaps, and what the review panel narrowed.

What the figures show​

  • Track: one Annex B engagement of the test seed (353), chosen by a rule in the script (the median engagement among the stored three-period ones): truth red, ownship blue, ctl alone per period orange, the joint solve green and dashed through the gaps.
  • Verdict: ctl alone ÷ joint in range on every split with 95% engagement intervals, on the registered rows and on rows the period determines alone.
  • Kinds: the same for periods with and without an ownship turn of their own.
  • Gaps: true manoeuvres inside gaps found and missed, and the share of quiet gaps with an invented manoeuvre.

Reproducing the figures​

uv run python scripts/research/tl8_charts.py --record experiments/20261118-tl8 --out-dir site/static/img/2026-11-18-joined-periods-slides

The script reads only the committed record (results branch results/timelate-tl-k-test-44252585727); each figure's .json sidecar names the inputs' digests and the commit. Data: seed 353, 5-second bearings, configs/timelate/tl-joined-*.json, generated in the CI run.

item.title: Several periods of one target, joined through the gaps: a gain, mostly where a period could not stand alone
item.description: Contact on a target comes and goes. Every time-late study so far gave the standing system
item.content:encoded:
Contact on a target comes and goes. Every time-late study so far gave the standing system one period per target. This one gave it two or three periods of the same target, separated by gaps with no bearings, and asked whether one solve over the whole span, with the track continuous through the gaps, beats solving each period alone. By the rule registered beforehand it does, on all four splits and with no harm. The review panel approved and narrowed what that means: most of the gain is periods that cannot be solved alone becoming solvable. Nothing was trained. The illustrated companion is the slides post.

What was built​

The joint solve needed no new search. The standing control ctl (spec 016: the evidence search over manoeuvre histories with the arc model, wild bearings edited, declared at an evidence margin of 1) already handles missing bearings. Given the span from the first period's start to the last period's end, with the gaps' bearings marked missing, it runs unchanged. The arc model carries the track through each gap, and the search may place manoeuvres there.

Each engagement is laid out as two or three periods of 15 to 30 minutes with gaps of 5 to 30 minutes, from a random stream of its own. Three solves run on the same bearings:

  • each period alone;
  • the joint solve;
  • the span with every bearing (what the gaps cost).

Each period is scored on rows 30 s apart where the known-history bound from the span's bearings is below 0.5. Both sides use the same rows.

How it was decided, and the first registration that stopped​

The rule: the per-period ratio of median range error, alone ÷ joint, has its geometric mean over periods and a 95% interval from resampling engagements.

  • gain: the interval is wholly above 1;
  • harm: the interval is wholly below 1 in range, course or speed on any split.

The first registration stopped at validation (seed 350). Its soundness check read 0.75 against a band of 0.8 to 1.5. The check was a median over the rows of about twenty engagements, but a fit's rows share one error, so each engagement is in effect one draw. On tuning the check's own interval had already crossed the band's edge. That was my fault in the registration, not the reference's. With the owner's agreement it was re-registered (fresh seeds 352 and 353) with a statistic over engagements. It passed validation at 1.13 [0.80, 1.62] over 66 engagements. The test seed was scored once.

The result​

splitalone ÷ joint, rangeon rows a period determines alone
Annex B (decided)3.10 [2.22, 4.58]2.64 [1.68, 4.70]
busier targets1.97 [1.63, 2.39]1.28 [0.95, 1.75], not shown
2% wild bearings2.72 [2.04, 3.75]2.21 [1.52, 3.29]
held course12.8 [8.5, 20.4]3.56 [2.33, 5.43]

Gain on every split; no harm in any quantity. The median per-period ratio is 2.09 on Annex B and 1.69 on busier targets.

What it means, as the panel narrowed it​

  • Mostly an answer where there was none. Rows were chosen by the span's bound. On rows that only the joined data determine, ctl alone's median relative range error is about 0.46, the scoring cut-off: it had no estimate there. Periods without an ownship turn of their own gain 4.35 (Annex B). Periods with one gain 1.65 (Annex B) and 1.13 [0.90, 1.43] on busier targets, where no gain is shown. The difference between the two kinds of period is the one reading that is real on every split.
  • Held course is the easy case. On held course the whole span is one leg, which suits the model by construction. The 12.8 says nothing about how far the result reaches.
  • The splits are not independent. The wild-bearing split is Annex B's engagements with outliers added, and held course shares 69 of 70 layouts with Annex B.
  • One period in eight is twice as bad joined (12% Annex B, 15% busier). Nothing in the output says which.
  • Gap manoeuvres. Of true manoeuvres inside gaps the joint solve declares 40 of 43 (Annex B) but only 83 of 130 on busier targets (36% missed). It invents one in about a fifth of quiet gaps. An inferred gap manoeuvre looks the same in the output as an observed one.
  • What the gaps cost. With every bearing the span is solved about 1.6 times better (every bearing ÷ joint 0.61), but only on rows the gaps make hard. On rows a period determines alone the difference is not shown (0.86 [0.62, 1.18]).
  • The soundness check is a screen. It catches a reference that returns its start. It does not measure efficiency: a perfectly efficient reference reads about 0.79 under its own model, and the geometric mean hides runaway fits, which reach 773 on test.

So the outcome is narrower than "joining is three times better". Within these simulated conditions the joint solve is the standing time-late system for two or three periods of one target in at most two hours. The conditions are periods of 15 to 30 minutes, gaps of 5 to 30 minutes, certain association and Annex B manoeuvres in the gaps. It beats ignoring the other periods. Whether it beats carrying state from one window to the next (spec 024) is not tested.

Forecasts​

Right: Annex B about 3, wild bearings about 2.5, held course about 10, busier targets a gain.

Wrong:

  • a loss on busier periods with their own ownship turn: they came out level;
  • a loss on 10 to 20 minute gaps: they gained;
  • gaps costing a factor of two: it was about 1.6.

The held-course false-manoeuvre forecast (under 0.15) came out at 0.17, which is not separated from it.

What was not done​

  • No comparison with spec 024's carried state: it was not merged when the test ran.
  • No IMM or EKF tracks beside.
  • No test of the runner's slicing; a reviewer's check stands in.
  • Run-to-run variation between CI machines (about 8% on tuning) was not re-measured. It cannot change the verdict.
  • Gaps over 30 minutes, uncertain association across a gap and several targets are untested.

What next (the owner's choice)​

The panel's order:

  1. Score spec 024's carried state on these engagements.
  2. A per-period consistency flag and markers on inferred gap manoeuvres, measured first on spent seeds for whether the flag finds the twice-as-bad periods.
  3. A stated uncertainty for the joined track.
  4. A stress split with longer, busier gaps.
  5. Association across a gap is a scope question for the owner.

Records: decision experiments/20261118-tl8-decision2/ (the first, 20261118-tl8-decision/, stopped at 20261118-tl8-val/), validation 20261118-tl8-val2/, test 20261118-tl8/ with the panel's review.md, tuning 20261117-tl8-tuning/. Spec specs/025-joined-periods/.

item.title: Kickoff: long engagements, carrying state, an incremental C, realism
item.description: The owner asked for note 12's three recommendations to be implemented. They are: carry state
item.content:encoded:
The owner asked for note 12's three recommendations to be implemented. They are: carry state between time-late windows, make C incremental, and make the long engagements more realistic. Spec: specs/024-long-carry-incremental-realism/.

Where we are​

  • Spec 023 ran the standing systems on 6 to 48 hour engagements, on windows. The time-late control held 1.6–2.7% median range error. Each real-time estimate re-ran C over its 2-hour window (27–37 s). The scenario was kind: the ownship steered on the truth, contact was never lost, and there was one target.

Where this task moves to​

  • Carry: each time-late window also starts its search from the previous window's declared history, in place of the start from nothing. It is compared with ctl on every window.
  • Incremental C: one confirmation per 2-hour block of estimates. Each estimate keeps the confirmed legs inside its 2-hour window. For blocks of one estimate this equals spec 023's run.
  • Realism, from a random stream of its own, so the first target is spec 023's:
    • the ownship steers on measured bearings and a range belief with 30% error;
    • contact gaps, and detection that fades beyond about 40 km;
    • a second target that the ownship does not manoeuvre for, with bearings mis-associated where the two contacts cross.
  • Risks: the second contact may be held too rarely to score, and one engagement per length gives anecdotes, not rates. A registered study is proposed afterwards, not run.

How progress will be shown​

The slides post will carry:

  • ctl and ctl-carry error and run time by window;
  • the incremental run's cost per estimate beside spec 023's;
  • each engagement's realistic tracks for both contacts;
  • error against time with the gaps marked.

item.title: Slides: longer engagements, 6 to 48 hours
item.description: Issue #42 asked what it would take to run our TMA on engagements of 6 to 48 hours. On four
item.content:encoded:
Issue #42 asked what it would take to run our TMA on engagements of 6 to 48 hours. On four simulated engagements (seed 348), every standing system ran to the end, on windows of the size it was built for. The time-late control keeps its accuracy at every length. Running it on a whole long period does not work as written, and several parts of the code assume one ownship zig. An investigation, not a gate. Spec: specs/023-long-engagements/.

What was built​

  • A long-engagement simulator (src/tma2/long/sim.py), separate from generator 0.6.0, whose output stays byte-identical. The target follows Annex B's statistics. The ownship turns at the start of each 20–40 minute leg and keeps the target at 3–25 km, steering on the true target position.
  • Windows (src/tma2/long/windows.py) in the form every estimator already reads, and C″'s zig veto applied at every ownship turn.
  • Real-time and time-late runners (src/tma2/long/realtime.py, timelate.py), the tma2-long CLI and the long.yml workflow.
  • Long-engagement sections on the viewer and the time-late page, precomputed in Python.
  • Research note 12 (docs/research/12-long-engagements.md) and the record experiments/20261117-long/ (tables.md generated from summary.json).

What was found​

6 h12 h24 h48 h
time-late ctl, median range error2.0%1.9%2.7%1.6%
time-late C″20.5%15.0%8.5%9.0%
real-time E, every 10 min17.4%17.5%14.3%20.9%
real-time C″23.2%17.1%13.2%19.9%
real-time IMM (answered)19.0% (1.00)35.2% (1.00)15.0% (0.96)30.9% (0.81)
  • ctl on one long period: 1 min for half an hour, 114 min for 6 hours, and at most ten manoeuvres (6 hours held 16).
  • The real-time model re-solves its 2-hour window for every estimate: 27–37 s on one core.
  • The IMM over the whole engagement took 426 s at 48 hours against 6 s at 6; the cause is not established.
  • The Cramér–Rao bound over a whole engagement needs 4.5 GB at 48 hours.

What was not achieved​

  • One engagement per duration: these are anecdotes, not rates.
  • The scenario is kind: the ownship steers on the truth, contact is never lost, one target.
  • No whole-engagement solve, and E does not run in the browser on these engagements.

What comes next (the owner's choice)​

Recommended: carry state between windows (each window starts from the previous solution), then an incremental C so a real-time estimate costs the same at hour 48 as at hour 2; realism (an ownship steering on its own solution, contact gaps, a second target) before any registered study. The next fresh seed is 349.

Figures: scripts/research/long_charts.py, with a sidecar beside each SVG.

item.title: Kickoff: longer engagements, 6 to 48 hours
item.description: Issue #42 asks what it takes to apply our TMA to engagements of 6, 12, 24 and 48 hours, and to
item.content:encoded:
Issue #42 asks what it takes to apply our TMA to engagements of 6, 12, 24 and 48 hours, and to show them on the viewer and time-late pages. This task is an investigation: it simulates one engagement of each length, runs the standing systems on them as they are, measures what that costs and how they do, and lists the implementation challenges. Spec: specs/023-long-engagements/.

Where we are​

  • Every engagement so far is 40 to 120 minutes with one ownship zig (MAN2, generator 0.6.0).
  • The real-time model E (Gate 2) is carried and runs in the browser. Its exported graph takes exactly 720 rows: two hours of 10-second bearings.
  • The time-late track closed with the classical control ctl standing, decided on periods of 20 to 120 minutes.

Where this task moves to​

  • Acceptance (no gate, nothing trained, no GPU):
    • four engagements (seed 348, fresh) of 6, 12, 24 and 48 hours, with Annex B's target manoeuvres and an ownship that turns at each 20–40 minute leg and keeps the target in range;
    • every system runs to the end of each: real-time every 10 minutes on a sliding 2-hour window (E, C″, one leg) and over the whole engagement (IMM); time-late ctl on a chain of 2-hour windows, stitched;
    • a research note listing the challenges, each measured where it can be;
    • long-engagement sections on /viewer and /timelate.
  • Plan:
    • a separate simulator, so generator 0.6.0 stays byte-identical (its table holds 32 target changes; 48 hours needs about 100);
    • windows cut from the long engagement in the form every estimator already reads;
    • the runs on CI (about 14 CPU-hours for the real-time part alone);
    • a timing of ctl on single periods of 0.5 to 6 hours, to show why it is run on windows.
  • Risks: ctl may be too slow on long periods to time at all; four engagements are anecdotes, so the note will not claim rates.

How progress will be shown​

The slides post will carry the tracks of the 48-hour engagement, error against time for each system, run time against period length, and the list of challenges.

item.title: Kickoff: time-late over several periods of one target, joined through the gaps
item.description: Contact on a target comes and goes. Until now every time-late study gave the standing system
item.content:encoded:
Contact on a target comes and goes. Until now every time-late study gave the standing system one period per target. This task gives it two or three periods of the same target separated by gaps with no bearings, and asks whether solving them together, with the target's track continuous through the gaps, gives each period a better whole-period solution than solving each alone. The owner chose it on 2026-11-17 (option C: motion continuity only, no target-specific prior). It is classical work on CPU; nothing is trained.

Where we are​

  • The time-late track was written up as a whole in the time-late account. The standing system is the classical control ctl (evidence-scored search over manoeuvre histories with the arc model, declared at an evidence margin of 1), with its recorded faults. A learned time-late model was not shown to help, at this budget.
  • The account named more information as one reason to look again: "several periods of the same target". This is that study.
  • Open: whatever a gap hides. A manoeuvre in a gap can only be inferred from how the periods disagree.

Where this task moves to​

  • SRD §1 (the time-late consumer), §5 (paired statistics, fresh seeds, registration before results), §9 (the owner's decision); spec folder specs/025-joined-periods/.
  • Judged by a rule registered before the fresh seeds exist: on each split, the paired per-period ratio of median range error, ctl alone ÷ joint, with an interval that resamples engagements. Gain if wholly above 1; harm if wholly below 1 in range, course or speed on any split.
  • Plan:
    1. Lay engagements out as two or three periods with gaps of about 5 to 30 minutes, from a stream of their own (the generator untouched).
    2. Build the joint solve: one search over histories across the whole span, with manoeuvres allowed in the gaps and bearings only in the periods.
    3. Tune span settings on seed 349; register the rule; validate on 350 (soundness); test on 351, once.
    4. Panel review, write-up and slides.
  • Risks: a long gap may leave the joined track no better constrained than the periods alone, and an invented manoeuvre in a gap may cost more than the join gains. We stop at validation if the span reference or the joint solve fails its soundness checks.

How progress will be shown​

  • Track plots of engagements with gaps: truth, ctl per period, the joint track (drawn through the gaps, dashed where there are no bearings), with true and declared manoeuvres.
  • Charts of the per-period ratio by split, by whether the period holds an ownship manoeuvre of its own, by gap length, and by whether the target manoeuvred in the gap.
  • Data: the test record on seed 351 (tuning 349, validation 350), Annex B, shifted-prior, wild-bearing and held-course splits.

item.title: Slides: the site, published, with persistent PR previews
item.description: The site is published to GitHub Pages on every merge. A new time-late page shows
item.content:encoded:
The site is published to GitHub Pages on every merge. A new time-late page shows the standing time-late system's tracks. Every pull request now keeps a preview, listed on PR previews. Spec: specs/022-site-publishing/.

What was built​

  • .github/workflows/pages.yml:
    • Merges to main publish the site at the root of gh-pages.
    • Each same-repository PR publishes its own build at pr/<n>/, and the copy is kept after the PR completes.
    • Closing a PR updates its state in pr/index.json.
    • A manual run builds a preview for an earlier PR.
    • Deploys run one at a time.
  • /previews lists every PR with a preview: its state, a link to the preview, and links to the blog posts it added or changed, opened in that preview.
  • /timelate draws whole-period tracks from spec 016's test record (seed 341, used):
    • the 20 first stored periods each of Annex B targets, 2% wild bearings and a shifted manoeuvre prior;
    • the standing control, C″, the true-history fit and the learned model;
    • true and declared manoeuvres on a timeline;
    • per-period errors, checked against the record by a unit test.

What was not achieved​

  • PRs before this one have no preview until the manual backfill is run for them.
  • The page's medians are over every stored row, not the scorer's rows, so they are not the record's figures. The page says so.

item.title: Kickoff: publish the site, a time-late page, persistent PR previews
item.description: The site has been built in CI but never published. This task publishes it to GitHub Pages on
item.content:encoded:
The site has been built in CI but never published. This task publishes it to GitHub Pages on every merge. It adds a time-late page that shows the standing system's whole-period tracks, and gives every pull request a persistent preview, listed in an index. Spec: specs/022-site-publishing/.

Where we are​

  • Specs 020 and 021 put the carried model in the browser. The time-late account closed the time-late track with a classical control standing.
  • None of this is online. gh-pages holds only the first commit's README.

Where this task moves to​

  • Acceptance:
    • after a merge, the root, the blog, /viewer, /timelate and /previews return 200;
    • a PR's preview and its post links work while it is open and after it is merged;
    • the time-late page's errors equal the record's, recomputed.
  • Plan:
    • a pages.yml workflow deploys to gh-pages: the root on main, and pr/<n>/ for each same-repository PR;
    • an index file and a /previews page;
    • the time-late page, from spec 016's test record;
    • a manual backfill for earlier PRs.
  • Risks: the branch grows by a site per PR, though git stores identical files once. Pages must serve the gh-pages branch. It does today, since it serves the README.

How progress will be shown​

The PR for this task is the first with a preview. Its slides post links the published pages.

Updates​

  • 2026-11-16, after the owner's review of the preview:
    • The time-late page shows each system's solution whole, as one fit to all the period's bearings. The time slider is gone; start and end markers and 10-minute ticks remain.
    • The viewer says it is the real-time model and points to the time-late page.
  • 2026-11-17, issue 44: each PR now carries a comment linking its preview at pr/<n>/, the blog posts it adds or changes and the commit it was built from. One comment per PR, found by a hidden marker and edited in place on every push, as the argonautical repository does it. A backfill run publishes without commenting.
  • 2026-11-17, issue 41 (the owner's request):
    • The track plots (the viewer, time-late and the long-engagement sections on both pages) zoom with the mouse wheel about the cursor. A drag pans, a double click resets, and buttons do the same for touch and keyboard users. Markers and line widths keep their size; the scale bar follows the zoom.
    • The viewer can show the measured bearings received so far, one a minute with the latest in bold. They come from the engagement's scenario file, checked against the manifest's digest. The time-late data carry no bearings, so that page has zoom only.
    • Both plots now use one scale on both axes. Before, north–south was drawn at 0.79 (viewer) and 0.73 (time-late) of east–west, which bent courses and squashed the 1-σ ellipse.

item.title: Slides: the carried model end to end in the browser
item.description: The viewer can now run Gate 2's carried model live, from bearings alone. The
item.content:encoded:
The viewer can now run Gate 2's carried model live, from bearings alone. The classical segmenter C, E-s's evidence and E-w's estimate all run in the browser. On 30 check scenarios every decision matches Python's. Spec: specs/021-browser-segmenter/. Record: experiments/20261116-port/.

What was built​

  • A JavaScript port of C's host code from its frozen Python (site/static/viewer-data/js/):
    • the per-row least squares and the GLR statistic;
    • the ownship segmenter O and E-s's features;
    • the search, its Levenberg–Marquardt segment costs and the dynamic programme;
    • nominations, confirmation, intervals and the hand-over.
  • The physics layer at confirmation's settings, exported as its own graph. Its three-runtime conformance passes, with cost agreeing to 7e-15 in the browser.
  • A live mode on the page: a module worker runs the whole pipeline with progress and a cancel, draws the live trail beside the others, and compares it with Python.
  • The checks:
    • a committed dump of every intermediate for 30 scenarios of used seed 319;
    • a Node comparison stage by stage (CI job browser-port);
    • live mode on every demo engagement in Chromium (viewer_leg.mjs).

What the figures show​

  • Agreement: identical segmentations on 1,770 of 1,770 scored rows, for C and for E.

  • Margins: the largest difference in a confirmation cost drop per scenario, against the smallest margin of any decision from its threshold.

    • The differences are 5.4e-9 or less, except one of 1.3e-4.
    • The margins are 0.152 or more.

    The gap explains the identity. It does not guarantee it: an engagement with a decision within 1e-3 of its threshold could differ, and the check would say so.

  • Stages: live mode takes 25 to 93 s an engagement on one WASM thread. Confirmation is most of it. The first row waits for confirmation: about 76 s on the busiest engagement, which misses the spec's one-minute target for the first row.

What was not achieved​

  • Pasting a scenario of one's own (the spec's third story, P3) is not built.

  • Some intermediates differ without changing a decision:

    • one row's least squares on ordinal 22 lands in another minimum;
    • search cost tables differ by up to 22% where fits hit their iteration cap.
    • the GLR statistic differs by up to 2.9. At one row (ordinal 1, row 256) it lies on the other side of the alarm threshold from Python's. No nomination changed there, but one could on another scenario, and the check would fail.

    These are recorded in the research notes, not hidden.

What comes next​

The owner's choice. The remaining options from spec 020's write-up are real data, several periods of one target, and ownship advice.

item.title: Kickoff: the carried model end to end in the browser
item.description: The owner chose to port the classical segmenter C to JavaScript, so that the
item.content:encoded:
The owner chose to port the classical segmenter C to JavaScript, so that the viewer runs the carried model from bearings alone, with nothing prepared in Python. Spec: specs/021-browser-segmenter/. Nothing is trained, no gate, no fresh seed.

Where we are​

  • Spec 020's viewer runs E-w's exported graph in the browser, on C's hand-over shipped from Python. CI checks it against Python to 3e-6 on 181 rows.
  • The carried model is still Gate 2's E: E-s's evidence, C's confirmation, and E-w into the physics layer. E-s and E-w are exported graphs. C is Python.

Where this task moves to​

  • SRD §1 (the viewer) and constitution VI (the browser as a runtime).
  • Acceptance:
    • on at least 30 scenarios of seed 319, the browser's segmentation equals Python's on at least 95% of scored rows;
    • every difference is traced to a decision near its threshold;
    • the live estimate matches Python's where the segmentation does;
    • the busiest demo engagement finishes in under 10 minutes on a CI runner.
  • Plan:
    1. Export the physics layer as a cost graph, with three-runtime conformance.
    2. Port C's host code to JavaScript: LS states, GLR, search, confirmation, hand-over.
    3. Write a Python dump of every intermediate and a headless comparison, stage by stage.
    4. Add a live mode on the page, and pasted scenarios if time allows.
    5. Slides.
  • Risks:
    • Speed. C's confirmation needs about 600 physics-layer rows on a busy engagement, about 2.5 minutes in the browser, and E's segmentation as much again.
    • Fragile decisions. A threshold decision can flip on last-bit differences, so the claim is "identical except near the threshold", with the margins reported.
  • Stop condition: if the port cannot reach 95% identical rows for reasons other than near-threshold decisions, the record says so and the page keeps the shipped mode as its default.

How progress will be shown​

  • Each stage's agreement with Python (statistic, costs, decisions) on the check scenarios.
  • The share of identical rows.
  • Every near-threshold decision with its margin.
  • Stage times per engagement.
  • A track plot from live mode beside the shipped one.
